introduction: “If but one ray from the divine name ‘the Beautiful’ is manifested in a person, hearts and minds are seen to be attracted.” The guide starts from that attraction and asks where beauty really lies: in the face, which fades; in the pearl, which needs no silk; in the thing brought to its perfection; in the gardener’s heart before the garden. Plato’s ladder, Plotinus’s sculptor of the self, Augustine’s “Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new”, and the Bible’s preference for the heart over the appearance all climb the same way. But poets have defended the lower rungs. Herrick gathers the rosebuds because they die; Keats says a thing of beauty never passes into nothingness; Hopkins gives glory for whatever is dappled and strange; the lilies of the field are praised as they are. And Tolstoy’s frightened husband asks the hard question about art that reading 9 raises: how to tell the beauty that lifts from the beauty that only moves.
questions: Plato and the readings both rank inner beauty above outer. What, if anything, do the readings add to Plato’s ladder?
Herrick and Keats respond differently to the fading of beautiful things, and neither turns away. Does the guide’s preference for what does not fade do justice to what does?
Reading 9 distinguishes two kinds of beautiful order. How would you apply the distinction to a piece of music or a building you know?
“His outward garden must be a representative of his inner garden.” Is this true of artists in your experience? What would count against it?

outside.why: Outer beauty attracts, and inner beauty a thousand times more. Diotima’s ladder in Plato climbs the same way: he who has learned to see the beautiful in due order will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty.
The loved ones of God may not have “the best of looks”. Isaiah’s servant: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
A pearl’s lustre is its own, and silk would hide it. Peter: let it not be that outward adorning, but the hidden man of the heart, the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.
Physical beauty is “the reflection of water and color cast upon dust”. All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field.
Mortal comeliness passes. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.

“Roses shall give way to thorns.” Herrick from the same roses: gather ye rosebuds while ye may; and this same flower that smiles today tomorrow will be dying. The reading turns from what fades; the poet turns toward it while it lasts. Which honours beauty more?
Keats will not grant the premise: a thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its loveliness increases; it will never pass into nothingness. Is there a sense in which he and the reading are both right?
Physical perfections are needed too. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
God loves each thing brought to “the highest” degree of its perfection. He hath made every thing beautiful in his time.
Craft is a gift. Of the maker of the tabernacle: I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in all manner of workmanship.

One kind of beautiful arrangement arouses worldly desire; another conforms to truth. Tolstoy’s Pozdnyshev fears all of it: music transports me into a state which is not my own; I seem to feel what I do not feel. Where do the readings draw the line he could not find?

“If the heart of a gardener is not an artistic garden in itself he will not be able to produce a single flower.” Plotinus: withdraw into yourself and look; and if you do not find yourself beautiful yet, act as does the creator of a statue that is to be made beautiful.
Flowers differing in colour and form heighten each other’s beauty. Hopkins: glory be to God for dappled things; all things counter, original, spare, strange.
